 PDD and Temu Top Singapore Shopping Apps. Is Shopee in Trouble?
 by 
 Joo Parn (JP) 
 November 19, 2026 
 in 
 Singapore , Stocks 
 0 
 Open the shopping charts on a Singapore phone this week and you might think the e-commerce war is over. On Apple’s App Store, Temu is the No. 1 free shopping app and Pinduoduo, its sister app in China, is No. 2. On Google Play, Temu carries the “#1 top free” badge in Shopping too.
 Shopee, the market leader, was fourth on the App Store, and second on Google Play.

 So is Shopee in trouble? The short answer is that the download charts say Temu is winning attention, but the usage and spending data say Shopee is still winning the customer, and its latest quarter was its most profitable ever.
 What the app charts actually show
 On Apple’s App Store, Temu and PDD have emerged as the top 2 apps under the shopping category. Shopee comes in fourth.
 On Google Play for the Android mobile platform, Temu takes the top spot too, but Shopee holds on to second, with TikTok Shop right behind in third.
 Some observations that stood out are the recurring appearances of Chinese platforms like Temu, PDD, Taobao and AliExpress. And not to mention Lazada and Amazon also appear on the lists. So if anyone is losing ground in downloads, it’s not only Shopee.
 Shopee’s numbers say otherwise
 Sea Ltd (NYSE: SE) reported its third quarter on 10 November. Shopee’s results do not look like a business losing customers.
 Shopee, Q3’26 Value Change 
 Gross merchandise value (GMV) US$39.7 billion +23% 
 Gross orders 4.5 billion +26% 
 Revenue US$6.1 billion +41% 
 Core marketplace revenue (fees and ads) US$4.6 billion +51% 
 Adjusted EBITDA US$269 million +45% (record) 
 Gross merchandise value grew by +23% and gross orders were up by +26%.
 Revenue growth achieved +41%, driven heavily by core marketplace revenue, which includes fees and ads. Adjusted EBITDA grew by +45%, a record.
 The Temu challenge is visible, but requires more observation. Shoppe’s orders are growing faster than its GMV, which means the average order is getting smaller. Management mentioned “more value-seeking behaviours in the market”, while Shopee is charging more, not less, as evidenced by the core marketplace revenue growing more than twice as fast as its GMV.
 It’s an inference, not a conclusion: a platform with real competitive pressure usually cuts fees to keep sellers and shoppers but Shopee is raising them. Profitability is also rising, as evidenced by adjusted EBITDA being about 0.68% of GMV, up from about 0.58% a year earlier arithmetically.
 While yes, there might be concern about what the App Store rankings show for Singapore, Singapore remains a small part of Shopee’s footprint, and Shopee commands a stronger presence in other Asian countries.
 Temu’s side of the story
 Temu is one of the new kids on the block, pushing hard into Southeast Asia, but its parent is under more pressure than SE.
 PDD Holdings Inc – ADR (NASDAQ: PDD) owns Temu, and Temu is PDD’s trump card to pivot, growing out of China after successfully disrupting Taobao and JD. However, all magnificent growth will eventually hit a ceiling. PDD looks to be hitting one now. In its April to June quarter, revenue grew by +8% to 112.4 billion yuan, below forecasts, while net profit fell -12% to 27.2 billion yuan.
 And while Temu has seen strong growth and presence in Malaysia and Singapore, its ASEAN growth blueprint is not fully unlocked. Indonesia has blocked Temu, so that’s one major market that Temu is absent from.
 Temu’s model is also different from Shopee’s. Shopee is a marketplace where local sellers, brands and its own logistics business compete on delivery speed and price. Temu, like Taobao, mostly ships directly from Chinese factories. Temu is sharper on price and ranges, but delivery would take some time for goods to arrive. Coupled with the ease of quickly canceling orders, cheaper does not always seem better if online buyers quickly u-turn on their impulses.
 So is Shopee in trouble?
 Not on the evidence available today.
 While Temu is winning downloads, it is likely spending heavily to do so. Yes, people will talk and share what they bought at what prices, and the growth will spread through word of mouth and via the group buying method, rooted in parent company PDD Holdings’ social commerce strategy.
 But where would online shoppers continue to buy their essentials or non-discretionary items? Seems like it’s still Shopee from the earnings, reports and metrics.
 While this is by no means an impregnable fort, the risk of David usurping Goliath is there. If Temu converts downloads into a habit among bargain hunters, the price-sensitive users will switch.
 And if buyers migrate, take rates will also need to be revised downwards to go head-to-head with Temu. This was visible when Shopee was muscling Lazada to be the go-to e-commerce marketplace.
 And the threats if any, should come from TikTok Shop first, rather than Temu. Momentum Works estimates TikTok Shop and Tokopedia combined are already about two thirds of Shopee’s size across Southeast Asia.
 For SE shareholders, Singapore is a small slice of Shopee. A Temu win in Singapore alone would not dent SE’s numbers or thesis.
 A Temu push across Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam would.
 My Opinion
 For investors investing long enough, I see the likes of PDD and Temu replaying the Shopee script when it bounced into the limelight.
 Crazy growth, solid gaming cash-generating pillar, and share prices that went to dizzying heights.
 I too thought that no one could beat and replicate SE.
 But as I observed and went through the selloffs myself, I opine that the e-commerce business model is really a red ocean playground. The challenger will always seduce users to switch over with better pricing and faster deliveries. The market leader would always need to find ways to defend their market share.
 SE could succumb and lose out, or it can still emerge as the go-to e-commerce platform.
 What I am trying to say, is that it’s not as moat-y as it looks. And to wrap it up, the wise Charlie Munger used to say this:
 “I got charmed by the idea of their position in the Chinese internet; I didn’t stop to realize they’re still a goddamn retailer. It’s going to be a competitive business, the internet.”
 Charlie Munger, 2023 
 I think he’s right. What do you think?
